clauses.reason: Executive Order 6206-A of July 16, 1933 states: "It is ordered that the condition heretofore imposed as to the termination of approval of the Code is now withdrawn and that the Code of Fair Competition for the Cotton Textile Industry is finally approved with the conditions so accepted and with the amendments so proposed, as set forth in Schedule A attached hereto." That command is a final approval, with amendments set out in Schedule A, of the Code of Fair Competition for the Cotton Textile Industry under section 3 of Title I of the National Industrial Recovery Act, and it has legal effect only through that approval: under section 3(b) the code's provisions became the standards of fair competition for the trade, and under sections 3(c) and 3(f) violations were restrainable in equity and punishable as misdemeanors. Section 2 of S.J. Res. 113, approved June 14, 1935, provides: "All the provisions of Title I of such Act delegating power to the President to approve or prescribe codes of fair competition and providing for the enforcement of such codes are hereby repealed". The resolution states no other effective date, so the command ended as a prospective operative command on June 14, 1935. No earlier end is shown (see earlier_end_check). The June 16, 1935 expiry is not an end because section 1 of the resolution replaced it with April 1, 1936. Schechter (295 U.S. 495, decided May 27, 1935) is recorded as a validity characterization, not an end date.

research_rationale:
Executive Order 6206-A (July 16, 1933) is a final approval, with amendments set out in Schedule A, of the Code of Fair Competition for the Cotton Textile Industry under section 3 of Title I of the National Industrial Recovery Act. Read in full from the held American Presidency Project transcription (page record checked; identity, date and subject confirmed against the census register and the WPA 1944 list); the withdrawal of the termination condition leaves the approval without a four-month end. Its command depends entirely on the code approval, so its first end is the repeal of the code-approval and code-enforcement provisions of Title I by section 2 of S.J. Res. 113 on June 14, 1935, applying SHARED_ANALYSIS.md and its adjudication; Schechter (May 27, 1935) is recorded as a validity characterization only.
Member checks: {"earlier_end_check":"The order withdraws the earlier condition that terminated approval at the end of four months unless expressly renewed (\"condition 12 of said order providing for the termination of approval at the end of four months unless expressly renewed\"), so no four-month end applies to this final approval. Paragraph 5 of Schedule A begins \"Until adoption of further provisions of this Code that may prove necessary\", which is a term of the code that depends on later code provisions and not a limit on the approval, and paragraph 1 asks a code agency to report \"prior to January 1, 1934\", which is a deadline and not an end. Held later orders naming the Cotton Textile Code are: EO 6242-C, 6242-D and 6242-E (denials of company applications for exemption, each excepting the Administrator's stay of July 30, 1933 on the machine-hour provision as applied to tire yarns); EO 6407 and EO 6476 (denial of that exemption and termination of the stay, effective November 13 and December 11, 1933); EO 6424 and EO 6463 (extensions of the stay's termination date); EO 6420-A (approval of modifications \"made a part of said code\"); EO 6858 (September 26, 1934: creates the Textile Labor Relations Board and, in section 9, abolishes the Cotton Textile National Industrial Relations Board created by section XVII of the code as amended July 10, 1934); and EO 6876 (approval of an amendment). I read the operative paragraph of each. None cancels, suspends as a whole, supersedes or revokes the code approval: the stays reached one provision as applied to one product line and ended in 1933, EO 6858 concerns a board of the code's labor administration created by a July 1934 amendment, and EO 6420-A and EO 6876 are amendments, which are later events. No held record shows this code cancelled, suspended, superseded or revoked before June 14, 1935, and none shows a modification under section 10(b) that reached this order's command. June 16, 1935 is not an end, because section 1 of S.J. Res. 113 replaced that expiry with April 1, 1936. Schechter (May 27, 1935) is a validity characterization, not an end date.","independent_command_check":"No appointment, delegation, direction to a government agency or other command independent of the code approval appears. The Planning and Fair Practice Agency named in Schedule A is an agency of the code itself, not of the government, and its report function exists only as a code term. The recital of the applicants' request and the Administrator's recommendation command nothing.","savings_check":"Read S.J. Res. 113 section 2 and its proviso and NIRA section 5 in the packet excerpts. No held source continues this approval, a prosecution under it or any command of this order after June 14, 1935; accrued acts, liabilities and the section 5 exemption for completed action are recorded as transferred or accrued and not as continued operation.","scope_check":"One operative command: withdrawal of the termination condition and final approval of the code with the conditions accepted and the amendments proposed. Schedule A (attached to the order) sets out those amendments, including paragraph 1 (a function of the code's Planning and Fair Practice Agency to consider employee home ownership and report) and paragraphs 2 to 6 (hours, wage differentials, stretch-out, operation of the code). Each item is a term of the code approved by this command, with no force apart from the approval, so the single clause covers it. The conditions in paragraphs 1, 3, 7, 8, 9 and 13 of the July 9, 1933 order that the applicants accepted are not held in text; the only condition the held order describes as terminating approval is condition 12, which it withdraws."}

savings.reason: Acts done and liabilities incurred under the approved code before June 14, 1935 are accrued consequences, and the section 5 exemption from the antitrust laws for action complying with an approved code taken while Title I was in effect is likewise an accrued effect for completed action. The proviso to section 2 of S.J. Res. 113 names agreements and action under them, not codes, and states no time limit; the held text does not settle whether it narrowed the section 5 exemption for past action under codes, and whatever exemption survives for past action is an accrued effect, not continued operation of this approval. Nothing in the held sources continues the approval after June 14, 1935.

source_notes.date_qualification: 1935-05-27: date the section 3 delegation was declared unconstitutional; validity characterization (void from issuance under then-prevailing doctrine), not an end date
source_notes.reason: Schechter, 295 U.S. 495, held the code provisions in question invalid on both of its grounds; recorded as a validity characterization of section 3 code approvals, not as an end date for this order. It adjudicated the Live Poultry Code provisions and cancelled or withdrew no other approving order.

source_notes.date_qualification: 1933-06-16: date the Act was approved; states the repealed legal effects of a code approval, not an end date
source_notes.reason: Sections 3(a)-(f) state the legal effects of an approved code that section 2 of S.J. Res. 113 repealed: the code's provisions became the standards of fair competition (3(b)), district courts could restrain violations (3(c)), and violations were misdemeanors (3(f)).
